subject: Modern History
sub_topic: Gandhi's early career — South Africa, Champaran, Kheda

concepts.name: Gandhi's Arrival in South Africa and the Natal Incident (1893)
key_dimensions: Circumstances: Legal work for Dada Abdulla & Co. — not a political mission initially
Pietermaritzburg railway incident: ejection from first-class compartment — the transformative moment
Distinction between this personal humiliation and the broader systemic racism Gandhi later fought
UPSC trap: Gandhi went to South Africa in 1893, NOT as a political activist — the evolution of purpose

concepts.name: Natal Indian Congress (NIC) — Formation and Significance (1894)
key_dimensions: Founded by Gandhi in 1894 — his FIRST organisational experiment in political mobilisation
Purpose: oppose the Natal Legislative Assembly Bill disenfranchising Indians
NIC as a precursor to INC methods: petitions, memorials, press campaigns
Contrast with later Satyagraha methods — NIC relied on constitutional/moderate methods
UPSC trap: NIC ≠ Indian National Congress; confusion between the two bodies

concepts.name: Indentured Labour System in South Africa and Gandhi's Response
key_dimensions: £3 annual tax on indentured Indians in Natal — a key grievance Gandhi championed
Distinction between 'free Indians' (merchants, professionals) and indentured labourers — Gandhi initially more focused on former
Gandhi's evolving solidarity: from elite Indian merchants to working-class indentured labourers
Abolition of indentured labour system: Gandhi's campaign contributed to its end in 1917 in India (Champaran link)
UPSC trap: Indentured system abolished in India in 1917, not in South Africa — context matters

concepts.name: Satyagraha: Conceptual Origins and First Application in South Africa
key_dimensions: Etymology: 'Satya' (truth) + 'Agraha' (insistence/force) — coined by Gandhi, replacing 'passive resistance'
Why Gandhi rejected 'passive resistance': it implied weakness and could be used with hatred; Satyagraha requires love
First organised Satyagraha: against the Asiatic Registration Act (Black Act) of Transvaal, 1906
Core principle: suffering of the Satyagrahi converts the opponent — not coercion but moral persuasion
UPSC trap: Satyagraha ≠ passive resistance; Gandhi explicitly distinguished them — a frequent MCQ angle

concepts.name: Asiatic Registration Act (Black Act), Transvaal, 1906 — The First Satyagraha Campaign
key_dimensions: Provisions: compulsory registration and fingerprinting of all Indians in Transvaal
Gandhi's response: mass pledge at Empire Theatre, Johannesburg (September 1906) — collective non-compliance
Outcome and compromise: temporary agreement with General Smuts — subsequently violated by Smuts (Gandhi called it his first experience of broken promises)
Significance: tested mass non-violent resistance for the first time — template for Indian campaigns
UPSC trap: This is the FIRST Satyagraha, not Champaran — Champaran was first in India

concepts.name: Phoenix Settlement and Tolstoy Farm — Gandhi's Experiments in Community Living
key_dimensions: Phoenix Settlement (1904, Natal): inspired by Ruskin's 'Unto This Last' — manual labour, self-sufficiency, equality
Tolstoy Farm (1910, Transvaal): named after Leo Tolstoy — housed Satyagrahis and their families during campaigns
Ideological influences: Ruskin (dignity of labour), Tolstoy (non-violence, simple living), Thoreau (civil disobedience)
Link to later Sabarmati and Sevagram Ashrams — continuity of Gandhi's communal living experiments
UPSC trap: Phoenix came before Tolstoy Farm; Ruskin inspired Phoenix, Tolstoy inspired the Farm

concepts.name: Gopal Krishna Gokhale's Visit to South Africa (1912) and Its Significance
key_dimensions: Gokhale visited South Africa in 1912 — inspected conditions of Indians, met with government officials
Gandhi considered Gokhale his political mentor ('my political guru')
Gokhale extracted a promise from the South African government to repeal the £3 tax — promise not kept
This experience reinforced Gandhi's distrust of government promises and the need for sustained Satyagraha
UPSC trap: Gokhale is Gandhi's guru in politics, not Raychandbhai (who was Gandhi's spiritual/moral mentor)

concepts.name: The Great March of 1913 — Culminating Campaign in South Africa
key_dimensions: Trigger: Supreme Court ruling invalidating all non-Christian marriages — affected Indian women's status
Gandhi led a march of over 2,000 indentured miners from Natal into Transvaal in November 1913
Significance: first time Gandhi led a mass movement including women and working-class Indians
Outcome: Gandhi–Smuts Agreement (1914) / Indians Relief Act, 1914 — abolished £3 tax, recognised Indian marriages
UPSC trap: Indians Relief Act 1914 was the outcome, not a unilateral government concession — negotiated settlement

concepts.name: Gandhi's Return to India (1915) and Gokhale's Advice
key_dimensions: Gandhi returned to India in January 1915 — received a hero's welcome
Gokhale's advice: travel across India for one year and observe before participating in politics ('year of political silence')
Gandhi founded Satyagraha Ashram at Kochrab, Ahmedabad (1915), later shifted to Sabarmati (1917)
Significance of the year of silence: Gandhi understood Indian poverty, caste, and rural conditions firsthand
UPSC trap: Gandhi did NOT immediately join INC politics in 1915 — he observed for a year per Gokhale's guidance

concepts.name: Champaran Satyagraha (1917) — Context and the Tinkathia System
key_dimensions: Tinkathia system: indigo cultivators forced to grow indigo on 3/20ths (teen kathha) of their land for European planters
Raj Kumar Shukla: the peasant who persuaded Gandhi to visit Champaran — symbol of grassroots mobilisation
Champaran was in Bihar — Gandhi's first direct engagement with Indian peasant/agrarian distress
UPSC trap: Tinkathia ≠ Ryotwari or Zamindari — it was a specific PLANTATION system unique to indigo districts

concepts.name: Champaran Inquiry and the Method of 'Constructive Investigation'
key_dimensions: Gandhi's approach: systematic recording of peasant testimonies before launching agitation — evidence-based Satyagraha
Government ordered Gandhi to leave Champaran — he refused, was arrested, triggering mass protests
Government appointed Champaran Agrarian Committee (1917) with Gandhi as a member — concession to public pressure
Outcome: Champaran Agrarian Act, 1918 — abolished Tinkathia system, provided compensation to peasants
UPSC trap: Gandhi was a MEMBER of the inquiry committee, not its chairman — he influenced but didn't head it

concepts.name: Champaran as First Civil Disobedience in India — Significance and Limitations
key_dimensions: Described by Gandhi as his 'first civil disobedience in India' — refusal to obey the order to leave Champaran
Tagore conferred the title 'Mahatma' on Gandhi around this period — popularisation of the honorific
Limitations: movement remained localised, did not escalate into a national campaign
Champaran demonstrated that Satyagraha could work in Indian conditions — proof of concept
UPSC trap: 'Mahatma' title — attributed to Tagore by common tradition, but Gandhi himself was uncomfortable with it

concepts.name: Kheda Satyagraha (1918) — Agrarian Distress and Revenue Remission Demand
key_dimensions: Context: crop failure in Kheda (Gujarat) in 1917–18; peasants demanded suspension of land revenue per government rules (if yield < 25% of normal, revenue could be suspended)
Government's refusal despite meeting the legal threshold — Gandhi's grievance
Method: no-revenue campaign; peasants asked to refuse payment, accept attachment of property
Vallabhbhai Patel's emergence: Kheda was his first major association with Gandhi — launched his political career
UPSC trap: Kheda demand was revenue SUSPENSION, not permanent abolition — a crucial distinction

concepts.name: Outcome of Kheda Satyagraha and Its Limitations
key_dimensions: Outcome was ambiguous: government quietly instructed collectors to recover revenue only from those who could pay — no formal written concession
Gandhi declared the movement successful; historians debate whether it was a genuine victory
Significance: demonstrated peasant capacity for organised non-violent resistance in India
Contrast with Champaran: Champaran had a clear legislative outcome (Agrarian Act 1918); Kheda had an informal administrative concession
UPSC trap: Kheda did NOT result in formal remission — government never officially acknowledged the peasants' demands

concepts.name: Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918) — Gandhi's Labour Satyagraha
key_dimensions: Issue: mill workers demanded 35% wage increase (plague bonus continuation); owners offered 20%
Gandhi's unique position: Anasuya Sarabhai (workers' leader) was sister of mill owner Ambalal Sarabhai — Gandhi mediated between them
Method: workers took a pledge not to resume work until demands were met; Gandhi undertook a fast
Gandhi's fast: first use of fast as a Satyagraha tool in India — controversial even then
Outcome: arbitration awarded 35% increase; UPSC trap: Ahmedabad strike is CONTEMPORANEOUS with Kheda (1918) — both happened in the same year

concepts.name: Gandhi's Relationship with the Indian National Congress Before 1919
key_dimensions: Gandhi attended INC sessions (e.g., Lucknow 1916) but did not take a leadership role
Lucknow Pact (1916): Gandhi was a witness to the Hindu–Muslim unity moment but was not a principal architect
Gandhi's divergence from Bal-Pal-Lal and Gokhale's moderate tradition: he synthesised both but went beyond both
Gandhi's mass mobilisation approach vs. INC's elite, urban, lawyer-dominated character pre-1919
UPSC trap: Gandhi did NOT lead INC before 1920 — his formal takeover of INC came with the Non-Cooperation Movement

concepts.name: Concept of 'Constructive Programme' — Origins in South Africa and Early India
key_dimensions: Constructive programme = positive, nation-building activities alongside agitation (khadi, village industries, communal harmony, sanitation)
Gandhi insisted agitation alone was insufficient — self-reliance and social reform must accompany political resistance
Origins traceable to Phoenix Settlement and Tolstoy Farm — productive self-sufficient communities
In Champaran: Gandhi set up schools, promoted sanitation, addressed untouchability alongside the agrarian agitation
UPSC trap: Constructive programme is NOT the same as Non-Cooperation — it is the complement to, not a substitute for, Satyagraha

concepts.name: Gandhi's Intellectual Influences — Ruskin, Thoreau, Tolstoy, and the Bhagavad Gita
key_dimensions: Ruskin's 'Unto This Last': converted Gandhi overnight — dignity of manual labour, equal value of all work (inspired Phoenix Settlement)
Thoreau's 'Civil Disobedience': Gandhi acknowledged influence but argued his Satyagraha was more positive and love-based
Tolstoy's 'The Kingdom of God Is Within You': radical non-violence, rejection of state coercion (inspired Tolstoy Farm)
Bhagavad Gita: Gandhi's 'spiritual reference book' — nishkama karma (desireless action) underpinned his method
UPSC trap: Gandhi did NOT coin 'civil disobedience' — it comes from Thoreau; Gandhi preferred 'civil resistance' or 'Satyagraha'

concepts.name: Role of Women in Early Gandhian Campaigns — South Africa and India
key_dimensions: South Africa 1913: Indian women (including Kasturba Gandhi) crossed the Natal–Transvaal border in deliberate violation of the law — novel use of women in protest
Ahmedabad 1918: Anasuya Sarabhai led mill workers — one of the first women to lead a Gandhian labour movement
Gandhi's deliberate inclusion of women: broke from elite nationalist tradition that kept women at home
Limitation: women's participation was often framed by Gandhi in terms of their 'moral purity' and sacrifice — not gender equality per se
UPSC trap: Women's mass participation in Indian nationalism is traced to Gandhi's campaigns, NOT to the earlier moderate or extremist phases

concepts.name: Champaran–Kheda–Ahmedabad Triad (1917–18) — Comparative Analysis and Strategic Significance
key_dimensions: Three simultaneous campaigns in 1917–18: peasant (Champaran), peasant revenue (Kheda), labour (Ahmedabad) — Gandhi fought on three fronts
Common thread: all used Satyagraha but with different specific methods (inquiry, no-revenue, strike/fast)
Each introduced a key associate: Champaran → Rajendra Prasad & J.B. Kripalani; Kheda → Vallabhbhai Patel; Ahmedabad → Anasuya Sarabhai
Strategic significance: proved Satyagraha's applicability across different social classes (peasants AND industrial workers) and regions
UPSC trap: These three movements are pre-Rowlatt — Gandhi was still operating on LOCAL/regional issues, NOT yet leading a NATIONAL mass movement
